name: Chilli Paneer
cuisine: Indo-Chinese (born in Kolkata's Chinese community, now on every Indian "Chinese" menu, from Mumbai street carts to restaurants; also "paneer chilli", "chilly paneer", "cheese chilli" in Kolkata)

ingredients.name: Sunflower oil (groundnut oil also used; it adds a peanut allergen), for shallow-frying
Onion (pyaz/kanda)
ingredients.householdMeasure: ½ small onion, cut in 1-inch petals

ingredients.name: Spring onion (hara pyaz)
ingredients.householdMeasure: 2 tbsp chopped, whites and greens kept apart

ingredients.name: Cornflour, for slurry (optional, for gloss)
ingredients.householdMeasure: ½ tsp, mixed in 2 tbsp water

equipment: 2 small bowls (batter; sauce mix) and a cup for the slurry
Small kadai or 8-inch pan for shallow-frying
Slotted spoon or tongs, and a plate lined with paper towel (or a steel strainer)
Wok or large kadai for the toss

steps.title: Cut the paneer
steps.text: Cut 100 g paneer into 1-inch cubes.
steps.tip: If the paneer is hard from the fridge, soak the cubes in warm water for 10 min, then pat dry. Soft paneer stays soft after frying.
steps.visualCue: About 12 even cubes with clean, sharp edges, none crumbling
steps.videoShot: The knife slicing the block into strips, then cubes.
steps.watchOut: Crumbly edges and uneven sizes, which fry unevenly (small bits burn while big cubes stay pale). If the block crumbles, the knife is blunt or the paneer is too fresh and soft; chill it for 15 min and cut again with a sawing motion.

steps.title: Pat the cubes dry
steps.text: Press them gently between paper towels.
steps.visualCue: No wet shine on the surface; the towel stops picking up moisture
steps.videoShot: A towel pressing on the cubes.
steps.watchOut: Wet cubes make the batter slide off and spit hot oil in the pan. If the batter later looks patchy on the cubes, they were not dry enough; pat again before coating.

steps.title: Mix the dry coating
steps.text: In a bowl, mix 1½ tbsp cornflour, 1 tbsp maida, ¼ tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, a pinch of pepper and a pinch of salt.
steps.visualCue: An even, pale pink powder with no red streaks
steps.videoShot: A spoon stirring the dry mix.
steps.watchOut: Streaks of red powder mean uneven seasoning, so some cubes taste bland and others sharp. Stir with a fork until the colour is the same everywhere.

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.text: Add ½ tsp ginger-garlic paste and about 2 tbsp water, a little at a time, and whisk.
steps.visualCue: Smooth, lump-free, thick enough to coat the back of a spoon (like thick buttermilk)
steps.videoShot: The spoon lifted to show the batter coating it.
steps.watchOut: Too much water gives a thin batter that runs off and fries into a soggy, bare shell; add a teaspoon of cornflour to rescue it. Too little leaves dry lumps; add water by the teaspoon.

steps.title: Coat the paneer
steps.text: Add the cubes and turn them until every side is covered.
steps.visualCue: All cubes evenly coated in a thin, pale layer, no white patches
steps.cameraCheck: The coated cubes in the bowl
steps.videoShot: Fingers or a spoon turning the cubes.
steps.watchOut: Thick, clumpy coats that turn doughy inside the crust, and cubes stuck together. Lift each cube and let the extra batter drip off before it goes in the oil.

steps.title: Chop the aromatics
steps.text: Finely chop 2 garlic cloves and the ½-inch ginger; slit 1 green chilli.
steps.visualCue: Tiny, even pieces of garlic and ginger, each about the size of a grain of rice
steps.cameraCheck: The small heaps on the board
steps.videoShot: The knife rocking through the garlic.
steps.watchOut: Big, uneven garlic pieces, which burn at the edges before the middle cooks, leaving a bitter taste. Re-chop any chunky pieces.

steps.title: Cut the vegetables
steps.text: Cut 50 g onion into 1-inch petals and 50 g capsicum into 1-inch squares. Chop 2 tbsp spring onion, keeping whites and greens separate.
steps.visualCue: Similar-sized pieces, close to the size of the paneer cubes
steps.cameraCheck: Onion, capsicum and spring onion side by side
steps.videoShot: Onion layers separated into petals.
steps.watchOut: Thin slices, which go limp and watery in the wok. Cut them thick so they stay crunchy, and keep the greens separate because they wilt in seconds.

steps.title: Mix the sauces
steps.text: In a small bowl, stir 2 tsp soy sauce, 1½ tsp red chilli sauce, 1½ tsp ketchup, 1 tsp vinegar and ¼ tsp sugar.
steps.tip: Having the sauce ready means the toss takes under 2 minutes and nothing burns.
steps.visualCue: A glossy, dark red-brown sauce with no ketchup streaks
steps.videoShot: Each sauce poured in, then stirred.
steps.watchOut: Too much soy and chilli sauce makes the plate too salty, and the sauce cannot be diluted once on the paneer. Measure with spoons and, if it tastes harsh, stir in 1 tsp water.

steps.title: Make the slurry (optional)
steps.text: Stir ½ tsp cornflour into 2 tbsp water.
steps.visualCue: Milky white, no lumps, and no powder settled at the bottom
steps.videoShot: A spoon stirring the white liquid.
steps.watchOut: Cornflour sinks within seconds, so an unstirred slurry pours out as clear water and the sauce stays thin. Stir it again right before pouring.

steps.title: Heat the frying oil
steps.text: Pour 60 ml (¼ cup) oil into the small kadai and heat on medium-high.
steps.visualCue: A drop of batter rises to the top in 2–3 seconds with steady bubbles
steps.videoShot: Batter drop sizzling up to the surface.
steps.watchOut: Oil that is too cool (the drop sinks and sits) makes greasy, soggy paneer; oil that smokes or browns the drop at once will burn the coat before it cooks. Lower the flame if it smokes and wait a minute.

steps.title: Fry the paneer
steps.text: Lower the cubes in one by one, in a single layer. Fry, turning every minute.
steps.tip: Do not over-fry. After about 4 minutes the paneer turns chewy. Fry in 2 batches if they crowd the pan.
steps.visualCue: Light golden and crisp on all sides; bubbles slow down and the sizzle quietens
steps.cameraCheck: The cubes in the oil, turned to show a golden side
steps.videoShot: Tongs flipping a golden cube.
steps.watchOut: Over-frying, which turns paneer chewy and rubbery (darker than light gold), and crowding, which drops the oil temperature and gives pale, soggy cubes. Fry in 2 batches and lift out as soon as the sides are light gold.

steps.title: Drain the paneer
steps.text: Lift the cubes onto the paper-towel plate.
steps.tip: Let the frying oil cool and strain it for later; it is not counted in the nutrition (only about 12 g is absorbed, est.).
steps.visualCue: Crisp shell, no pooled oil on the plate
steps.videoShot: Slotted spoon lifting cubes out.
steps.watchOut: Stacking the cubes, which traps steam so the crust turns soft. Spread them in one layer and use the next 4 minutes for the toss.

steps.title: Heat the wok
steps.text: Put the wok on high heat and add 1 tsp oil.
steps.visualCue: The oil shimmers and gives off a faint wisp of smoke
steps.videoShot: The oil swirled around the wok.
steps.watchOut: A wok that is not hot enough, which steams the vegetables instead of searing them, so they turn limp and watery. Wait for the first wisp of smoke before adding anything.

steps.title: Fry the aromatics
steps.text: Add the garlic, ginger and green chilli. Stir.
steps.tip: Garlic burns fast on high heat. If it browns, lower the flame for a moment.
steps.visualCue: Garlic turns pale gold within seconds; strong garlic smell
steps.videoShot: Spatula stirring the sizzling garlic.
steps.watchOut: Brown or black garlic smells acrid and makes the whole dish bitter. If it browns before the vegetables go in, lift the wok off the heat for a moment, or start again with fresh garlic.

steps.title: Add the onion and spring onion whites
steps.text: Stir-fry on high.
steps.visualCue: Onion edges turn translucent but the petals still look firm and crunchy
steps.videoShot: Onion petals tossed in the wok.
steps.watchOut: Cooking until soft and brown, which makes the dish sweet and mushy. Stay under a minute; the onion finishes cooking in the sauce heat.

steps.title: Add the capsicum
steps.text: Stir-fry on high.
steps.visualCue: Capsicum turns bright green with a few charred spots; still crisp
steps.videoShot: Capsicum tossed with the onion.
steps.watchOut: Dull, olive-green, wrinkled capsicum is overcooked and releases water. Keep stirring on high and move on once it turns bright green.

steps.title: Add the sauce mix
steps.text: Pour it in and stir for a few seconds.
steps.visualCue: The sauce bubbles at once and coats the vegetables; sharp vinegar smell that fades in seconds
steps.videoShot: Sauce poured over the vegetables.
steps.watchOut: Leaving the sauce to boil down on high heat, which makes it salty and sticky or burnt at the edges. Stir for only 10–15 seconds, then move straight to the next step.

steps.title: Add the slurry (optional)
steps.text: Stir the slurry and pour it in, stirring constantly.
steps.tip: For a drier, crisper finish, skip the slurry; the chilli sauce has enough starch to coat.
steps.visualCue: The sauce turns glossy and thick, clinging to the vegetables
steps.videoShot: The sauce thickening as the spatula moves.
steps.watchOut: Lumpy, jelly-like sauce, which means too much slurry or no stirring. Stir fast; if it is too thick, splash in 1 tbsp water.

steps.title: Toss in the paneer
steps.text: Add the fried paneer, a pinch of pepper, and toss.
steps.visualCue: Every cube coated in a thin red-brown glaze, no sauce pooling at the bottom
steps.cameraCheck: The coated paneer in the wok
steps.videoShot: The wok tossed so the paneer flips.
steps.watchOut: Tossing for too long, which makes the crust soak up sauce and turn soggy, with cubes breaking apart. Toss for under 45 seconds and plate straight away.

steps.title: Finish and plate
steps.text: Turn off the heat, sprinkle the spring onion greens, and plate at once.
steps.visualCue: Glossy cubes with bright green flecks
steps.videoShot: Spring onion greens falling on the plate.
steps.watchOut: Adding the greens while the heat is still on, which wilts them to a dull olive colour. Switch off the flame first, then sprinkle.

The platform values are inconsistent, so treat none of them as reliable.

protein.source: same Swiggy listing (implausibly low for a paneer dish; conflicts with 33.17 g seen last cycle).

reasons: 100 g paneer gives a good 18–22 g of protein, and the onion and capsicum add some crunch and vitamin C. But paneer is high in saturated fat, the batter is refined flour and starch, the cubes are fried, and the bottled sauces bring about 1,050 mg sodium and some sugar. Fibre is low (about 3 g). Restaurant versions are usually deep-fried in reused oil, use thicker batter and more sauce, and often add MSG; one platform listing for a restaurant version shows implausible figures, so no restaurant fat figure can be relied on.

researchRating.basis: chilli paneer is one of India's best-loved Indo-Chinese starters, on almost every Indian "Chinese" menu and a party favourite. Recipe pages re-checked this cycle score very high (Hebbar's Kitchen 4.98/5 from 292 votes; Swasthi's Indian Healthy Recipes 4.98/5 from 422 votes on its combined dry and gravy card; Spice Up The Curry 4.67/5 from 9 votes), though a few lesser sites show lower scores on tiny samples (Zayka Ka Tadka gravy version 3.4/5 from 14 ratings; SideChef 4.3 from 3). Small deductions because many cooks complain of rubbery or soggy paneer, and it is widely seen as an indulgent, oily dish.

storage: Best eaten fresh; the coating goes soft within 30 minutes. Leftovers keep in an airtight box in the fridge for up to 2 days. Freezing is not recommended (the paneer turns spongy and the vegetables go limp). Reheat in a hot pan or wok for 1–2 minutes on high, or in an air fryer at 180 °C for 3–4 minutes to bring back some crispness; the microwave makes the coating soggy and the paneer rubbery.
leftoverRemix: Chilli paneer frankie. Warm a roti or paratha on a tawa, spread 1 tsp green chutney or a thin layer of hung curd, add the reheated chilli paneer and a handful of shredded cabbage or sliced onion, squeeze lime over it, roll tightly and toast the roll seam-side down for 30 seconds.
burnOff: about 8.2 km of running (575 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 11.5 km of brisk walking (about 2 hours 20 min at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.). The air-fryer version (about 505 kcal) is about 7.2 km of running.

navratri.reason: onion, garlic, maida, cornflour, soy sauce, ketchup and vinegar are not allowed under the common vrat rule set (assumed; families differ)

ekadashi.reason: flour coating, soy sauce and onion/garlic are commonly avoided on Ekadashi (common rule set assumed; families differ)

jain.reason: drop onion, garlic, fresh ginger, ginger-garlic paste and spring onion; add hing and sonth (see Jain variant)

ramadan.reason: vegetarian, so no halal-meat issue; protein-rich and good for iftar, but fried, oily and salty (about 1,050 mg sodium), so heavy for sehri

jain.reason: drop the onion (50 g), garlic (6 g), fresh ginger (3 g), ginger-garlic paste (3 g) and spring onion (15 g), all roots or bulbs; use extra capsicum, a pinch of hing and a pinch of sonth (see Jain variant)

vegan.reason: paneer is dairy (a tofu version is a different dish, chilli tofu)

pescatarian.reason: vegetarian recipe with no meat, fish or egg

sattvik.reason: drop the onion, garlic, ginger-garlic paste and spring onion; use hing and extra capsicum (see Jain variant)

glutenFree.reason: maida (8 g) and soy sauce both contain wheat; use cornflour only and gluten-free soy sauce or tamari, and check the chilli sauce and vinegar labels (see Gluten-free variant)

variants.reason: the dish is defined by paneer; chilli tofu (for example Ministry of Curry's chilli tofu, Bless My Food By Payal's vegan air-fryer chilli tofu) is an established, separate dish
the dish is paneer, which is dairy; the tofu version is a different dish
